lessons.title: bo po mo fo · wo
lessons.focus: All four tones, side by side; b vs p (the puff of air); the o that sounds like wo
lessons.goal: Hear bo po mo fo and wo in all four tones, hear b from p, and tell the four tones apart, one at a time and two or three in a row.

steps.title: The Pinyin chart
steps.text:
Every Chinese syllable is built the same way: an **initial** (the consonant at the start), a **final** (the rest) and a **tone** (the pitch).

The Pinyin chart lists all of them, about 400. Each of the first lessons teaches one group of initials.

Today: the lips, **b p m f**, with the final **o**. After b p m f the o has a little *w* in front: **bo** sounds like *b-wo*. The o itself is open, like British English *law* or German *Sonne*, but longer.

With no initial, the w is written out: **wo**.

steps.title: b and p: the puff of air
steps.text:
Hold your hand in front of your mouth.

**p** comes with a strong puff of air, like English *pie* or a firm German *P*.

**b** has no puff. It isn't a buzzing English *b* either: think of the *p* in English *spy*, or a soft southern German *b*.

**m** and **f** are the same as in English and German.

steps.title: Every syllable has a tone
steps.text:
A tone is a pitch shape. Change the tone and you get a different syllable, with a different meaning. Here is **mo** in the four tones. Just listen.

You'll always practise all four together: hearing them side by side is how you learn to tell them apart.

steps.title: 1st tone: high and flat
steps.text:
Start high and hold it, like singing one note.

English: the *Aaah* at the doctor's. German: a sung *Laaa*.

The mark is a flat line: **ō**. As a number: **o1**. The top row has all four tones to compare.

steps.title: 2nd tone: rising
steps.text:
Start in the middle and go up, like a surprised *What?* German: *Was?*, or *Ja?* answering the phone.

The mark rises from left to right: **ó**. As a number: **o2**.

steps.title: 3rd tone: low
steps.text:
Drop your voice low and keep it relaxed. A bit creaky is fine.

English: a low, doubtful *Hmm…* German: a reluctant *Na ja…*

Said on its own it dips and comes back up at the end, and it's the longest tone. Inside a sentence it mostly just stays **low**, so think *low*, not *down-up*.

The mark is a little valley: **ǒ**. As a number: **o3**.

steps.title: 4th tone: a sharp fall
steps.text:
Start high and drop fast, like a firm *No!* German: *Nein!* or *Doch!* It's the shortest tone.

The mark falls from left to right: **ò**. As a number: **o4**.

steps.title: Your first block of the chart
steps.text: Tap a square to hear it. Tap a syllable on the left to hear it in all four tones, or a tone at the top to hear the whole column. Draw the shapes in the air with your hand: high, rising, low, falling.

steps.title: wo: the o on its own
steps.text:
With no initial in front, the o of bo po mo fo is written **wo**: the little *w* you hear after b p m f, now on its own. It sounds like English *war* without the r.

Top row: **wo** in the four tones. Below: **mo** against **wo**, and **bo** against **wo**.

steps.title: Tones in a row
steps.text:
In real speech, syllables come one after another, and you have to catch each tone on the way. Now you'll hear two or three sounds in a row and pick the Pinyin that says them, in that order.

Follow the shape of each one: high, rising, low or falling. Play each row with ▶.

lessons.title: de te ne le · me · e
lessons.focus: The vowel e; d vs t; the 2nd tone against the 3rd
lessons.goal: Hear de te ne le and e in all four tones, hear d from t, and hear the 2nd tone from the 3rd, alone and in pairs.

steps.title: Warm-up
steps.text: First a quick look back: **b p m f** with **o**, in all four tones.

steps.title: A new vowel: e
steps.text:
The Chinese **e** isn't the e of English *bed* or German *Bett*.

Say **o**, then keep your tongue where it is and spread your lips into a smile. What comes out is a deep *uh*, a bit like English *duh*, or *her* in British English without the r.

Top row: **e** in the four tones. Below: **wo** against **e**.

(After the lips there's also **me**, but only as a light, toneless little word. You'll hear it later.)

steps.title: d and t: the puff again
steps.text:
It works like b and p: **t** has a strong puff of air (English *top*), **d** has none (the *t* in English *stop*).

**n** and **l** are the same as in English and German.

steps.title: 2nd or 3rd?
steps.text:
The pair beginners mix up most is the **2nd** tone (rising) and the **3rd** (low). Said on its own, the 3rd tone comes back up at the end, so both seem to go up.

Listen to where they **start**: the 2nd starts in the middle and climbs straight up, like a surprised *What?* The 3rd first sinks low and stays there a while, like a doubtful *Hmm…*

Each row is 2nd, then 3rd.

steps.title: Your second block of the chart
steps.text: de te ne le in all four tones. Play each row and draw the shapes in the air with your hand: high, rising, low, falling.

steps.title: Rising and low, in a row
steps.text:
Now the 2nd and the 3rd tone one after the other. In each pair, listen for the one that climbs **straight away** (2nd) and the one that sinks first (3rd).

Play each row with ▶.

lessons.title: ge ke he
lessons.focus: g vs k; the rough h; the 4th tone against the 3rd and the 1st
lessons.goal: Hear ge ke he in all four tones, hear g from k, and hear the 4th tone from the 3rd and the 1st, alone and in a row.

steps.title: Warm-up
steps.text: A quick look back at P02: **de te ne le** and **e**, in all four tones.

steps.title: 3rd or 4th?
steps.text:
Both can sound like they go down, but they start in different places.

The **4th** starts **high** and drops fast, like a firm *No!* (German *Nein!*). It's the shortest tone.

The **3rd** starts **low**, sinks even lower, then comes back up, like a doubtful *Hmm…?* (German *Naja…*). Said on its own it's the longest tone.

The marks draw the shapes: **ˋ** slopes down (lè), **ˇ** is a little valley, down and up again (lě).

Each row is 3rd, then 4th.

steps.title: g and k: the puff, a third time
steps.text:
Today: the back of the tongue, **g k h**, with the **e** from P02.

**g** and **k** are a pair like b/p and d/t. **k** has a strong puff of air (English *kite*, German *Kuh*). **g** has none: it's the *k* in English *sky*, not the buzzing *g* of English *go*.

Hand in front of your mouth again: you should only feel air on the k.

steps.title: h: rough, from the back
steps.text:
The Chinese **h** is made further back than an English h, with a bit of friction. It's close to the German *ch* in *ach* or *Bach* (not the soft one in *ich*), just a little lighter. English has nothing like it; Scottish *loch* comes close.

Top row: **he** in the four tones. Below: **ke** against **he**.

steps.title: 1st or 4th?
steps.text:
The 1st and the 4th tone both **start high**. The difference is what comes next: the 1st **stays** up, like one long sung note; the 4th **drops** fast, like a firm *No!*

Said quickly, a 1st tone can sound a little like a 4th. Listen to the end of the syllable: level, or falling?

Each row is 1st, then 4th.

steps.title: Your third block of the chart
steps.text: ge ke he in all four tones. Play each column too: four times high, four times rising, and so on.

steps.title: Low or falling, in a row
steps.text:
Now the 3rd and the 4th tone one after the other, with a 1st tone now and then. The 3rd stays **low** and comes back up at the end; the 4th starts **high** and drops; the 1st stays high.

Play each row with ▶.

lessons.title: ze ce se
lessons.focus: z = a soft German z (ts), c = ts with a puff, s always sharp; z vs c vs d and t
lessons.goal: Hear ze ce se in all four tones, and hear z from c and s, and both from d and t.

steps.title: Warm-up
steps.text: A quick look back at P03: **ge ke he** in all four tones.

steps.title: z: a soft ts
steps.text:
Today: the tongue tip at the teeth, **z c s**, with **e** again.

**z** is a *ts*, like the German *z* in *Zeit*, or the *ts* in English *cats*. It's soft, with **no puff** of air: closer to the *ds* in English *kids*. It's never the buzzing English *z* of *zoo*.

Top row: **ze** in two tones. Below: **de** against **ze**.

steps.title: c: ts with a puff
steps.text:
**c** is never a k or an s. It's **ts with a strong puff** of air, like a firm German *z* in *Zahn* with extra breath, or the *ts h* in English *its high*.

So z and c are a pair, like d/t and g/k: the same sound, without and with a puff.

steps.title: s: always sharp
steps.text:
**s** is always a sharp, hissing s, as in English *see* or German *ß* and *ss* (*Straße*, *muss*). It's never the soft German s of *Sonne* or *Rose*, even at the start of a syllable.

The row: **se**, **ce**, **ze**.

steps.title: Your fourth block of the chart
steps.text: ze ce se in all four tones. Say each one after the audio: z soft, c with a puff, s sharp.

steps.title: Same tone, different start
steps.text: In each row the tone stays the same and only the initial changes. Listen to the very start of each sound: soft **z**, puffed **c**, sharp **s**, and **d** and **t** from P02 to compare.

lessons.title: zhe che she re
lessons.focus: The tongue curled back; ze vs zhe, se vs she
lessons.goal: Hear zhe che she re in all four tones, hear ze from zhe, se from she and re from le.

steps.title: Warm-up
steps.text: A quick look back at P04: **ze ce se** in all four tones.

steps.title: The tongue curled back
steps.text:
Today: **zh ch sh r**. For all four, curl the tip of your tongue up and back, behind the bump above your top teeth. That gives them a darker, hollow sound.

- **zh** like the *j* in English *jam*, without the buzz; German *dsch*.
- **ch** like English *church*, with a puff; German *tsch*.
- **sh** like English *shoe*, German *sch*.
- **r** like the English *r* in *run*, with a little buzz, a bit like the *s* in *pleasure*. Never a German r.

They're written with two letters but are one sound each.

steps.title: z or zh? s or sh?
steps.text:
z c s (tongue at the teeth) and zh ch sh (tongue curled back) are the pairs most learners mix up. z c s are bright and hissing; zh ch sh are darker and hushing.

Each row is the tongue at the teeth, then curled back.

steps.title: Your fifth block of the chart
steps.text: zhe che she re in all four tones. Keep your tongue curled back the whole time.

steps.title: Bright or dark
steps.text:
Pairs in a row: one with the tongue at the teeth, one curled back. **z c s** are bright and hissing, **zh ch sh** dark and hushing.

And **r** against **l**: for l the tongue tip touches behind the top teeth; for r it's curled back and doesn't touch anything.

lessons.title: ji qi xi
lessons.focus: The flat tongue; j vs q; xi vs se vs she
lessons.goal: Hear ji qi xi in all four tones, hear j from q, and xi from se and she: all three tongue positions.

steps.title: Warm-up
steps.text: A quick look back at P05: **zhe che she re** in all four tones.

steps.title: A new vowel: i
steps.text:
Today: the tongue flat, **j q x**, with the final **i**.

This **i** is the plain *ee* of English *see*, German *Liebe*. Lips spread, tongue high.

For **j q x**, keep the tip of your tongue down behind your lower teeth and press the middle of the tongue up. That's what *flat* means here. They sound soft and bright, almost like they have a little *y* in them.

steps.title: j and q: the puff, once more
steps.text:
**j** is like the *j* in English *jeep*, but without the buzz and with the tongue flat. **q** is the same with a strong puff, like *ch* in English *cheese* (German *tsch*, softer).

The letter q is the surprise: it's never a k sound.

steps.title: x: the German ch of ich
steps.text:
**x** is like the German *ch* in *ich* or *Milch*: tongue flat, air hissing over it. English has no such sound; it's between *s* and *sh*, as in *see* and *she* said at once.

Row by row: **xi** against **se** and **she** (s, curled-back sh, flat x).

steps.title: Three ways to say ts and ch
steps.text: You now know three tongue positions: at the teeth (**z c s**), curled back (**zh ch sh**), flat (**j q x**). Each row is one sound in all three positions. P08 practises them side by side.

steps.title: Your sixth block of the chart
steps.text: ji qi xi in all four tones. That's every initial of Mandarin.

steps.title: Flat, curled back or at the teeth
steps.text:
Now the flat tongue against the other two positions, and all four tones, in pairs and threes. **j q x** are soft and bright, **zh ch sh** dark, **z c s** sharp.

Play each row with ▶.

lessons.title: Recap: the puff of air
lessons.focus: b/p, d/t, g/k, z/c, zh/ch, j/q mixed, all four tones
lessons.goal: Hear the puff of air in all six pairs (b/p, d/t, g/k, z/c, zh/ch, j/q) in a random mix, alone and in a row, with all four tones.

steps.title: Recap: the puff of air
steps.text:
No new sounds today. You've met six pairs that differ only in a **puff of air**: the second of each pair has one, the first doesn't.

Hand in front of your mouth: b d g z zh j stay still, p t k c ch q blow. This lesson mixes them all up, in all four tones.

steps.title: Puff or no puff
steps.text: Three pairs in all four tones: without a puff, then with one.

steps.title: Puff and tone together
steps.text: Now both at once: which initial, and which tone? Take your time: listen to the start for the puff, then to the pitch.

steps.title: Puff in a row
steps.text:
Now pairs and threes in a row, puff and no puff mixed, in all four tones. Listen to the start of each sound for the puff, then to its pitch.

Play each row with ▶.

lessons.title: Recap: z, zh or j?
lessons.focus: z/zh/j, c/ch/q, s/sh/x and r mixed, all four tones, faster
lessons.goal: Hear the three tongue positions apart (z/zh/j, c/ch/q, s/sh/x) and r, in a random mix, alone and in a row, with all four tones.

steps.title: Recap: three tongue positions
steps.text:
No new sounds today. Mandarin has three tongue positions where English and German have about one:

- **z c s**: tip of the tongue at the teeth. Bright and hissing.
- **zh ch sh r**: tip curled back. Dark and hushing.
- **j q x**: tip down, tongue flat. Soft, with a little *y* in it, like German *ich*.

Each row is one sound in the three positions.

steps.title: s, sh or x?
steps.text:
The hissing three are the hardest to hear apart. **s** is sharp and thin, **sh** is darker and lower, **x** is soft and light, like *ich*.

And **r** sits with sh: same curled-back tongue, but with a buzz.

steps.title: Three positions
steps.text: The tongue at the teeth, curled back and flat, in all four tones. Play the rows in pairs: ze then zhe, se then she.

steps.title: Faster: sound and tone
steps.text: The same mix with all four tones, a bit faster. Trust your first impression.

steps.title: Three in a row
steps.text:
The three positions one after another, then mixed with other sounds and all four tones. Trust your first impression.

Play each row with ▶.
